claims.claim: Wolfe writes in his foreword to Soldier of the Mist that the narrator recorded place names as he believed he understood their meanings, so the record's names are the narrator's guesses.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, foreword to Soldier of the Mist (Tor, 1986), p. xii, quoted by Scott Wowra in Ultan's Library, 7 September 2016
claims.quote: he understood (or believed he understood) their meanings

claims.claim: Wowra finds that folk etymology, a plausible but wrong translation, is the main way Wolfe's amnesiac narrator generates the place names in his record.
claims.source: Scott Wowra, 'Place Names in Gene Wolfe's Soldier of the Mist', Ultan's Library, 7 September 2016
claims.quote: it is the primary method Latro uses to record his place names

claims.claim: Wolfe says in a 1988 interview that his narrator arrives at the right meaning of a city's name by an incorrect derivation.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Darrell Schweitzer, Weird Tales, Spring 1988, quoted by Scott Wowra in Ultan's Library, 7 September 2016
claims.quote: although his derivation of it is incorrect

claims.claim: Wowra describes Wolfe's toponyms in Soldier of the Mist as plain compounded names such as Hundred Eyed and Redface Island that provoke wonder and puzzlement.
claims.quote: awash with charming place names that evoke wonder and puzzlement

claims.claim: Wolfe explains in his introduction that his narrator named a region Silent Country after mishearing a remark about a person's laconic manners.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, introduction to Soldier of the Mist (Tor, 1986), p. xii, quoted by Scott Wowra in Ultan's Library, 7 September 2016
claims.quote: seems to have heard some taciturn person referred to as

claims.claim: Wowra concludes that the record's place names are dominated by folk etymology, with descriptive, associative and commemorative naming used less often.
claims.quote: Latro relies predominantly on folk etymology

claims.claim: Gevers argues that Wolfe writes so that any seemingly incidental paragraph reflects the whole design, which is what obliges the reader to read incidental detail as evidence.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur: Beginnings and Endings in Gene Wolfe's The Book of the Long Sun', written 1998, published in Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: every paragraph, however incidental seeming, reflects the whole

claims.claim: Gevers argues that the divination scenes inside The Book of the Long Sun function as instruction to the reader in how closely the text must be read.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: instruction in, the demands of incisive reading

claims.claim: Gevers finds that every volume of The Book of the Long Sun opens with a dialogue in which the informed party releases what he knows only in oracular or obscure form.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: which he will only yield up in oracular or otherwise obscure form

claims.claim: Gevers describes Wolfe's narration in the final volume of the Long Sun as spare and unexplanatory, made of hints and implications.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: narration becomes spare, unexplanatory, a minefield of hints and implications

claims.claim: Gevers uses Kim Stanley Robinson and John Clute's term slingshot ending for a close whose implications carry past the end of the text.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: an ending whose momentum of implication carries well beyond the confines

claims.claim: Gevers notes that the narrator of The Book of the Long Sun identifies himself only in the last pages, which forces the reader to re-appraise everything already read.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: thus forcing the reader to re-appraise the whole of the preceding text

claims.claim: Gevers states that Wolfe's third volume instructs the reader to assemble the meaning of the text out of clues that appear disconnected.
claims.source: Nick Gevers, 'The Reader as Augur', Ultan's Library, 5 September 2000
claims.quote: assembling the meaning of the text from numerous seemingly disconnected clues

claims.claim: Borski endorses Wright's finding that the absence of any discourse between coloniser and colonised in The Fifth Head of Cerberus destabilises the reality the book reports.
claims.source: Robert Borski, 'Desanctifying Victor Trenchard', Ultan's Library, 24 May 2002 (dated December 2001)
claims.quote: the destabilizing effects such omissions have on reality

claims.claim: Borski links two of Wolfe's characters into a single pattern using small domestic repetitions, among them the barley soup each is served in prison.
claims.source: Robert Borski, 'Desanctifying Victor Trenchard', Ultan's Library, 24 May 2002
claims.quote: Both men are served barley soup while imprisoned

verdicts.trueWording: translated them when he understood (or believed he understood) their meanings
verdicts.note: Raw page (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200) quotes Wolfe's Foreword, Soldier of the Mist 1986 p.xii verbatim: 'In dealing with place names, I have followed the original writer, who sometimes wrote them as he heard them but more often translated them when he understood (or believed he understood) their meanings.' Wowra's own thesis ('folk etymology... the primary method Latro uses') supports the 'guesses' limb. Minor: Wolfe adds that some names were written as heard, so not every name is a guess; the article elsewhere calls the same p.xii text the 'Introduction'.

verdicts.trueWording: folk etymology is the primary method Latro uses
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the page: 'This process of translation is referred to as folk etymology, and it is the primary method Latro uses to record his place names.' The 'plausible but wrong' limb is the page's own definition ('a reasonable, but technically inaccurate, translation'); the 'amnesiac' limb is supported by 'Latro's recurrent, yet fleeting, awareness of his amnesia'.

verdicts.trueWording: he's right... although his derivation of it is incorrect
verdicts.note: Verbatim inside the block quote from Darrell Schweitzer's interview, Weird Tales Spring 1988, reproduced by Wowra: 'Latro calls Athens Thought because that's what he thinks it means. As it turns out, he's right. That is what it means, although his derivation of it is incorrect.' The city is Athens; the wrong derivation is athanatos.

verdicts.trueWording: awash with charming place names that evoke wonder and puzzlement
verdicts.note: The quote is the article's opening sentence, verbatim, and it does cite 'Hundred Eyed' and 'Redface Island' as its two examples. But Wowra nowhere characterises the toponyms as plain or as compounds: his words are 'charming', 'intriguing and idiosyncratic labels'. That descriptive limb is the claimant's, not the page's.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: described by Wowra as 'plain compounded names'

verdicts.trueWording: heard a person called Laconic and concluded Laconia meant Silent Country
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the page: Wolfe (1986, xii) 'explains in his introduction, "Latro seems to have heard some taciturn person referred to as having Laconic manners, and to have concluded that Laconia meant 'Silent Country.'"' The error Wolfe describes is inferential, not auditory: Latro hears 'Laconic manners' accurately and draws a false etymology. Region and name (Laconia / Silent Country) are confirmed by the folk-etymology table.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: mishearing — the page has Latro hearing the remark correctly and mis-inferring from it

verdicts.trueWording: predominantly folk etymology, less descriptive, associative, commemorative
verdicts.note: Conclusion, verbatim: 'Latro relies predominantly on folk etymology, and to a lesser extent on descriptive, associative, and commemorative derivations'. The same ranking is stated earlier: 'The predominant category is folk etymology, followed by the less frequent use of descriptive, associative, and commemorative place names.'

verdicts.trueWording: every paragraph, however incidental seeming, reflects the whole
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the augury paragraph: Silk's random-page reading is 'an initiation of the reader into the sort of intensive and ingenious textual decoding that Wolfe expects, and a warning that such alertness to symbolic implication and nuance must be exercised at all times, as every paragraph, however incidental seeming, reflects the whole.' Both limbs (design, and the duty it imposes on the reader) are on the page; cf. the New Sun hologram conceit, 'any fragment contains the essence of the whole'.

verdicts.trueWording: augury is a metaphor for, and instruction in, incisive reading
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'often in his text, augury is a metaphor for, and instruction in, the demands of incisive reading.' The 'scenes' limb is supported: 'scenes of formal augury are found in each volume of Long Sun... he accords augury a genuine prophetic function - most likely so that it can summarise the virtues of close reading.'

verdicts.trueWording: each opening passage features a dialogue... only yielded in oracular form
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'each opening passage features a dialogue between a more-or-less naive individual and a figure possessing privileged information, which he will only yield up in oracular or otherwise obscure form.' Gevers then walks all four volumes (Outsider/Silk, Horn/Silk, Quetzal/Remora, Potto/Mint), so 'every volume' holds.

verdicts.trueWording: narration becomes spare, unexplanatory, a minefield of hints and implications
verdicts.note: Verbatim, and it sits inside the paragraph beginning 'Volume four's plot is indeed complex' - volume four being Exodus From the Long Sun, the final volume of the tetralogy, so the 'final volume' limb is anchored.

verdicts.trueWording: Robinson and Clute's 'slingshot ending'; implication carries beyond the text
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'in what Kim Stanley Robinson and John Clute term a "slingshot ending", an ending whose momentum of implication carries well beyond the confines of the text it terminates.' Attribution of the term to Robinson and Clute is the page's own.

verdicts.trueWording: Horn identifies himself as narrator, forcing re-appraisal of the whole
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'After Horn has identified himself as the narrator of Long Sun in the section entitled "My Defense" (pp. 370-382), thus forcing the reader to re-appraise the whole of the preceding text'. The 'only in the last pages' limb is supported by the placement (Exodus's concluding section, of a volume ending at p.383) and by the earlier phrase 'his craftily concealed and long-term function as Long Sun's narrator'.

verdicts.trueWording: volume three's instructions: assemble meaning from seemingly disconnected clues
verdicts.note: Verbatim: Quetzal's remarks 'state volume three's operating instructions to the reader: the necessity of assembling the meaning of the text from numerous seemingly disconnected clues, the need to trust the narrator no further than necessary'. Volume three is Calde of the Long Sun, matching the claim's 'third volume'.

verdicts.trueWording: lack of discourse between colonizer and colonized... well argued and apposite
verdicts.note: Verbatim in Borski's second paragraph: 'Most of the points he makes, especially about the lack of discourse between colonizer and colonized, and the destabilizing effects such omissions have on reality, are well argued and apposite'. Endorsement limb confirmed by 'well argued and apposite'. Wording note: Borski writes 'lack of discourse' (claim says 'absence of any discourse') and 'on reality' unqualified (claim glosses it as 'the reality the book reports') - same substance, slightly stronger in the claim.

verdicts.trueWording: Both men are served barley soup while imprisoned (list item 14)
verdicts.note: Item 14 of Borski's numbered list is verbatim: 'Both men are served barley soup while imprisoned.' The pattern limb is the list's stated purpose: 'Victor Trenchard and Number Five are symbolic twins, with life circumstances and ultimate fates irrevocably linked'. Note the list is not only small domestic detail - it also rests on major parallels (each kills an alternate version of himself, both arrested for Maitre's murder).
